Poll interference is hard. Fooling voters is easy
articles.summary: You’ve likely heard the ominous what-if scenarios about election disruptions in November: immigration agents or federal troops roaming polling places, federal officials seizing ballots and voting machines, and President Donald Trump issuing an executive order postponing or cancelling the election. Courts and legal experts have given solid reasons that each one of those potential election disruptions is unlikely. But the threats have served their purpose: People are harbouring doubts.The federal government doesn’t have to interfere with the mechanics of the voting process to disrupt the election. The easiest way for bad actors to interfere in the midterm elections right now is to let fear and distrust mess with our minds. By intimidating people into thinking they’ll face harassment at the polls or casting doubt on the integrity of the process, the administration is planting the seeds that the results can’t be trusted.I recently spoke with a naturalized US citizen from Venezuela who lives in Miami. She’s a young professional, married with kids, and until recently had been an active member of her local political party. She’s a reliable voter, but she told me she won’t be voting in person this year. The ICE raids that have terrorized her community have left her and her neighbors isolated and afraid.“I don’t want to go and vote in person, because I am terrified that they’re going to bring out the National Guard,” she told me. “You know, I have PTSD.”This is where Trump has brought us: US citizens fear risking their safety to exercise their constitutional right to vote.For the last 21 months, the federal government has mounted an unprecedented attack on state sovereignty over elections. Trump signed two executive orders that seek to radically dictate state election policy. The Department of Justice sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to gain access to sensitive voter data. The White House seized Georgia’s ballots from the 2020 election. And Trump tried to rehash his election conspiracy theories in a prime-time speech earlier this year.Judges from county courthouses to the US Supreme Court have rebuffed much of it. But the effort has undercut voter confidence. A University of Georgia survey of more than 11,000 voters found only 58% of Republicans, 63% of Democrats, and 49% of Independents trusted that votes would be counted accurately nationwide. And a recent poll from AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that only 34% of US adults trust government certifications of election results “a great deal” or “quite a bit,” down from 40% in 2024.Sometimes all it takes is a headline to sow doubt. That’s what happened in 2016 when Russian hackers got access to the Illinois state voter registration database. The hackers went unnoticed for weeks and only when they started accessing thousands of records per second did Illinois election officials shut the system down.“Russia wanted to be noticed,” said David Becker, who runs the non-partisan election watchdog site The Center for Election Innovation and Research. “They wanted the American people to think that our foreign adversaries had … the ability to change our elections.” Since then, US adversaries, particularly Russia, Iran and China, have focused on manipulating social media to make voters, particularly supporters of losing candidates, believe that their elections were stolen.Fortunately, millions of voters haven’t been intimidated by these global or domestic scare tactics. Records indicate that two weeks into early voting, an unprecedented number of votes have already been cast across the country, in many states exceeding records broken in 2018, 2022 and 2024.And in unprecedented fashion, state elections officials have locked arms in a bipartisan effort to resist any attempt by the administration to interfere.State officials are taking a traditional “all hazards approach,” said Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, who leads the National Association of Secretaries of State. They’re prepared to handle election disruptions involving everything from natural disasters and bomb threats to power outages. This year, he told me, they’ve added “federal interference.”States have amassed teams of lawyers who are prepared to act quickly in the unlikely event that federal troops do show up, said Becker. They are also prepared to get before a judge if federal officials attempt to seize election equipment and get a ruling “before the chain of custody is irrevocably damaged,” he explained.But as a reminder, it’s a crime for anyone to order federal troops to a polling place — a violation punishable by up to five years in prison, a fine and disqualification from public office. Federal laws bar Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents from the polls. And it’s logistically impossible for Trump to cancel an election because thousands of officials across the country control elections, not the White House.The internet is an inviting host for allowing the mischief to continue in the weeks ahead. Let’s keep our wits about us. Thank the hard-working elections officials who keep the system sound, and don’t be duped.

US visa curbs not aimed at India: Rubio
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated that the Trump's administration's ongoing clampdown on legal immigration is not a direct attack on India.In an interview with The Indian Express, Rubio said the changes were part of a broader effort to overhaul the US immigration system and are being applied globally.His comments came in response to a question about concerns among Indians, including students and the large diaspora in the US, over recent visa restrictions, the H-1B debate and a deepening anti-immigrant rhetoric. The question also referred to a recently foiled plot to attack a temple."So the first thing is that every country has to have immigration laws. If they don’t, they are not a sovereign country. And this is not about India; this applies globally," Rubio told The Indian Express.Rubio said that the US was dealing with the consequences of years of problems in its immigration system and argued that several immigration programmes had been abused. He also cited birth tourism as an example, saying it involved other countries rather than India."Frankly, we have seen many of these programmes being abused. Again, it is not unique to Indians or India," he said. "So we are trying to fix 20 years of neglect of an immigration system… and that is not targeted towards India," Rubio added.Why India feels the impactRubio acknowledged that changes to the US visa system can have a significant impact on Indians because of the large number of applicants from the country in some visa categories."Now, obviously, because of the developments, because of the ties between our countries, because of how developed your economy is, there are certain categories of visas that see a large number of Indians applying for," he said.The US, he said, still wants foreign students, workers, visitors and investors, but wants immigration to take place under laws that are followed."We want people to visit the United States. We want people to study in the United States. There are certain people that we want, that want to come work for a time in the United States. We want people to invest in the United States, and we are always going to have people immigrate to the United States," Rubio said."But we want it done through a system of laws that are complied with," he added.'Biggest threat to legal immigration is illegal immigration'Rubio also sought to draw a distinction between legal immigration and illegal immigration, arguing that large-scale unauthorised migration could undermine legal pathways."The biggest threat to legal immigration is illegal immigration. The biggest threat to legal immigration is mass migration, which again is not an Indian phenomenon (but) more unique to other parts of the world," he said.Rubio acknowledged that US policy changes could appear to be directed at India because of their effect on Indian applicants, but rejected that interpretation."And while I know that from your perspective here in India, it may seem targeted at India, (but) it’s not," he said."There is virtually no country on Earth that I visit where I don’t get a complaint about some visa or process, because we are fixing it globally."Rubio said the administration believed the changes would eventually make US immigration programmes more sustainable."Once it’s fixed, it will be far more sustainable. I actually think it will be better for the people using those programmes, and right and good for the United States," he said.

articles.title: France has a proud tradition of protesting
articles.summary: PARIS - No nation does mass protests quite like France.When the French fight high fuel taxes, they don yellow vests and march. When angry farmers want better pay, hundreds of them drive tractors down the Champs-Elysees. And when museum workers want better tourist management, they strike and shut down the Louvre.Passionate public protest is as French as "La Marseillaise," the 1792 anthem that enshrines the collective duty to fight tyranny in the country's national identity. But this month, the most violent demonstrations in years - and tough policing - have raised concern about riots overshadowing hundreds of thousands of peaceful demonstrators marching against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.Also read: France unrest leaves global brands with a burning problemOn Saturday alone, at least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings, looted stores and engulfed a historic city hall in flames. More protests could be in store."How can French people do this to France?" outgoing President Emmanuel Macron asked on Sunday. Nothing justifies the destruction, he added. "We all feel anger and shame."But any student of French history would know that the nation's proud, loud and colorful protest culture has sometimes turned violent - starting with the beheadings of King Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette during the revolution that overthrew the monarchy in 1789.A protest culture is bornHistorians say the revolution was where the modern-day French tradition of civic engagement as a duty was born. The idea is that voting is not the only way to drive change; demonstration is considered a bedrock value, a way to make elites hear the populace and to defend freedoms. The moment a child becomes an activist is seen as a generations-old rite of passage. The right to protest is even constitutionally protected."It's a way to build collective identity and political community," said Magali Della Sudda, research director in political science at the French National Center for Scientific Research in Bordeaux.France's post-revolution history is not a solid story of protests and reforms, but of cycles of popular uprisings, repression, mobilization and political concessions. The tradition has turned tragic; In 1871, government troops cracked down on the new "Paris Commune," or municipal government, reportedly killing thousands.In some ways, collective action won - as in 1968, when student demonstrations and a general strike forced the government to grant concessions like an increase in the minimum wage.In more recent history, the "yellow vests" - "gilets jaunes" in French - demonstrated against a proposed fuel tax increase, and that broadened into protests over other issues like living costs and inequality. Some demonstrations in 2018 and 2019 featured burning cars, looting and confrontations with police. It's not uncommon for French violence on the fringes to mar otherwise peaceful marches.Likewise, the student protests over the weekend expanded from education to other grievances - and featured dramatic scenes of looting and clashes with police. It's not clear how many of those who were ransacking shops had turned out to join the day's protest, which drew tens of thousands, or were mere opportunists. Authorities have responded with nightly curfews; there were calls for more protests later in the week.Also read: With France embroiled in protest, a look at the nation's economic standing by the numbersPolice violence blamed for mistrustSome of the forces driving protests for the last month owe to more recent French tradition, according to political scientist Fabien Jobard, who has studied the history of protest and policing.Since the 1990s, the country has seen recurring waves of what the French call "violences urbaines" and Americans would call riots, Jobard said. They are often sparked by police violence: nationwide unrest erupted in 2005 after two teenagers died while fleeing police, and again in 2023 after an officer fatally shot a 17-year-old during a traffic stop outside Paris."For young people from the suburbs, the riot is one of the traditional forms of collective expression," he said.Government critics and human rights campaigners have alleged that police tactics in the last month have been unnecessarily violent. Much of the criticism focuses on rubber-bullet launchers, known in France as LBDs, and stun grenades, which critics blame for serious injuries to protesters.And Della Sudda noted that the nearly 8,000 arrests in the weeks leading up to Oct. 17 dwarf the few dozen detained during a 1998 protest of 500,000 students against teacher shortages and dilapidated schools.The feeling of not being heard also is part of it, she says. Rather than listen to protesters and negotiate, Della Sudda noted for example, the government tried to appease "yellow vest" grievances through a digital platform, which translates to "the great national debate." Anti-government protesters panned Macron's plan."As a result," Della Sudda wrote, "mistrust is growing."

articles.title: Philanthropy’s biggest failure is its fear of failure
As slow as an India-US trade deal
articles.summary: There are forces who have probably been assigned the task of ensuring that Marco Rubio doesn't overhear this during the next few days he's here in India. But India is a big and loud place, and this corner column only mirrors it. So, consider our duty to put on record a new idiomatic phrase in English that has gained traction over the last few months: 'As slow as an India-US trade deal'.Those familiar with formulations such as 'watching paint dry' and 'waiting for Godot' may already know what we're talking about. Except, this latest idiom describes an activity that is simultaneously happening, not happening, and about to happen.Its most remarkable feature is its elasticity. A delayed flight is merely late. A delayed marriage may be called off. But something proceeding 'as slow as an India-US trade deal' enjoys permanent forward momentum without the inconvenience of arriving.Whenever an official announces that negotiations are 'almost complete', seasoned observers understand that it's nudge-nudge, wink-wink for another postponement. 'We are very close' means further away than previously feared. 'Final stages' suggests the beginning of another round. 'Constructive discussions' indicates that nobody has thrown a chair. Trade negotiators on both sides of the Indo-Pacific water table have finally produced something of lasting value: a phrase.

articles.title: France: Curfews bring calm to Paris
articles.summary: PARIS: Paris returned to calm on Tuesday after its first quiet night since a weekend marred by France's most destructive rioting in years, as authorities imposed curfews in several cities in an effort to prevent another round of rioting and looting.At least 2,400 people were arrested after rioters in cities across France on Saturday clashed with police, set cars on fire, stormed public buildings and engulfed a historic city hall in flames, during nationwide protests against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools.On Sunday evening, small groups set fire to trash bins, bicycles and other objects in the streets and looted businesses in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and other cities.Also Read: Paris police issue overnight curfew in 2 areas of French capital to try to prevent further disorderIn the capital, a curfew ran from 11 p.m. on Monday to 6 a.m. Tuesday, and a police helicopter circled over Place de la Republique overnight, a central point in the weekend clashes, sweeping the square with a searchlight to check that the order was being respected.Early Tuesday morning, workers used a crane to remove a giant fluorescent yellow vest draped over the statue at the center of the square, a reference to the " yellow vest " protests over fuel prices that began in 2018 and shook the first term of President Emmanuel Macron.Workers then used pressure washers to blast graffiti off the monument."The targeted curfews helped keep last night calm," Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Tuesday, adding that new curfews would be imposed that night "wherever the situation requires," decided locally by prefects, the state's representatives in each region, together with mayors.Speaking in Lille, northern France, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 149 people had been jailed nationwide as of Tuesday at noon. According to the Justice Ministry, of the roughly 2,500 people arrested since Saturday, more than 800 have been sent before prosecutors, most of whom were either put on trial immediately or ordered to appear at a later hearing.In Paris alone, about 300 people have been sent before prosecutors following the Oct. 17 protests, the city prosecutor's office said in a statement.Darmanin said he asked prosecutors to appeal any sentence they considered too lenient. "People with no criminal record ending up in prison for property crimes is extremely rare, if not unheard of," he said, arguing that the French justice system will be "extremely firm."In Lille, he said, three men aged 20 to 25 with no criminal record were each sentenced to 10 months in prison and imprisoned immediately for looting a video game store in the city's old town.The National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament, is launching an inquiry into the Oct. 17 violence and the authorities' policing strategy, its speaker, Yael Braun-Pivet, said, with findings expected "by the end of the year."

articles.title: Giant 'heat storms' are scorching the Earth
articles.summary: By Maurice Tamman, Ben Welsh, Pete Mckenzie, Charlie Szymanski, Delgerzaya Delgerjargal, Robbie Corey-Boulet, Loucoumane Coulibaly, Jeff Horwitz and Joan FausIn less than a lifetime, about six and a half decades, heat waves have evolved from sporadic, isolated episodes to massive, cascading weather events that can blanket vast swaths of the planet for months or even years at a time.The largest heat wave of the 1960s reached about 6% of the planet as it drifted for 46 days over the Atlantic Ocean, parts of Latin America and West Africa.The largest one this decade swept across almost 85% of the globe during its 367-day lifetime, stretching into the polar latitudes and touching virtually every human being on Earth.To continue calling such sprawling phenomena "heat waves" would be like calling a monsoon a rain shower. To understand the new reality of these immense expanses of heat, Reuters consulted with two dozen meteorologists and climate researchers - and analyzed temperatures for every hour of every day since 1960 for more than one million grid squares covering the entire globe. Out of those results we developed a new concept: the "heat storm."Simply put, heat storms are supersized heat waves. Reuters uses a conservative benchmark to define an ordinary heat wave: five or more consecutive days of abnormally high temperatures. Then we define the largest heat waves - those that at their peak cover at least 1% of the globe, roughly half the size of Canada - as heat storms.Applying this definition, Reuters identified a startling transformation. "Heat is the biggest killer from climate change," he said, noting that it can lead to "famine, hunger, death, conflict over resources."A NEW WAY TO UNDERSTAND CLIMATE CHANGEHeat storms constitute a new way to conceptualize how Earth's climate is changing as humanity pumps greenhouse gases into the atmosphere.The determination by climatologists that the average global temperature in 2025 was 1.47 C (2.6 F) above the pre-industrial level is useful to scientists and policymakers, but to many people it's so abstract as to be meaningless. What people do understand are heat waves - in Spanish, an "ola de calor"; in Arabic, a "mawjat hararia"; in Mandarin, a "re lang."Yet no universal definition of a heat wave exists. For example, authorities differ over duration: The US National Weather Service defines a heat wave as "abnormally and uncomfortably hot" weather typically lasting "two or more days," while the meteorological agencies of Australia, France, Spain and the United Kingdom set the threshold at three days. The temperature data comes from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts, and our detailed methodology is here. A heat wave occurs when the daily high temperature for any location reaches at least the 90th percentile of the historical range - in other words, the hottest 10% - for five days in a row.So a July heat wave in Istanbul is five or more consecutive days of at least 25.6 C (78.1 F), whereas one in Phoenix, Arizona, needs to reach 40.3 C (104.5 F).In Reuters' definition, a heat wave can happen in any season, so in Istanbul a January heat wave would be five consecutive days of at least (11.2 C) (52.2 F), and in Phoenix the threshold would be 20.8 C (69.4 F).To measure the geographical extent of heat waves, we map neighboring heat wave grid squares that form a cohesive area. Defining and naming heat storms is an important innovation, he added, and could help people to track impacts and consequences.As their numbers have swelled over the decades, heat storms and heat waves have not only caused individual catastrophes. They have also helped drive lasting, systemic effects.They exacerbate droughts and intensify fires - from Chile to Europe, the largest conflagrations on record happened during heat storms - and if they hit while a woman is pregnant, studies have found that she's more likely to suffer everything from stillbirth to preeclampsia, a leading killer of expecting and post-partum women.Warmer temperatures can usher in benefits, at least for some regions. Siberia now produces almost as much wheat as Russia's traditional breadbasket near the Black Sea. That's in part because increasing heat storms and heat waves have helped open far northern latitudes to agriculture while simultaneously contributing to droughts around the Black Sea that reduce production there.18 YEARS OF CONSTANT HEAT STORMSTens of thousands of ordinary heat waves flicker in and out of existence every year. Like heat storms, they too have escalated in number, more than doubling from the 1960s to this decade. The vast majority are small, however, never even covering 0.01% of the planet, about the size of a square that you could drive across in less than two and a half hours. Only a minuscule fraction of heat waves ever gets big enough to become heat storms, which currently number about 102 annually.Yet heat storms now claim the lion's share of Earth's unusually hot days, those in the top tenth of the historical range. In the 1960s, heat storms averaged 3% a year for any given spot on the planet. (The remainder comprised ordinary heatwaves and short bursts of heat that didn't last long enough to become a heatwave.)This decade, heat storms have accounted for almost 43% of such days.As greenhouse gas emissions have increased, so too have heat storms and ordinary heat waves. From the 1960s to this decade, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has increased by more than 30%. Over that time, the average portion of the planet likely to be covered by heat storms and heat waves has risen more than 12-fold. El Nino - the periodic episodes of unusually warm water in the Pacific Ocean that drive major weather patterns - has acted as an accelerant, intensifying heat storms and heat waves.Reuters has also examined the opposite of heat waves and heat storms - cold snaps and cold storms. They have dwindled. From the 1960s to this decade, the total area in a cold snap or cold storm on an average winter day has shrunk by almost 80%.Despite their mammoth scale, the phenomenon of heat storms has been largely invisible to the public. Until recent decades, heat storms were rarer and smaller, so easier to overlook.But perhaps as importantly, they hadn't been defined and named in the sharp way that typhoons and hurricanes are. Yes, people in Montreal, Perth and Hong Kong knew they were baking in a stretch of hot days - but they did not know that they were all experiencing one unitary heat storm.As part of this series examining heat storms and their effects, Reuters has integrated an online Heat Storm Tracker into our regular weather coverage. With this tool, people can see what had previously gone unnoticed and, using that knowledge, tally the impact of heat storms as they rage across regions.The rapid evolution of heat has not only made individual heat storms larger. Now, in sharp contrast to even 20 years ago, massive heat storms often run into, merge with, and split off from one another. For more than 18 years straight, 6,681 days, at least one heat storm has been roiling the planet, and often more than one.Many of them have been colossal. In the almost half century between 1960 and the start of the current 18-year cascade, only five heat storms had ever reached a peak size bigger than a tenth of the planet, about the area of Europe and Asia combined. As his illness worsened - swelling that began in his feet spread all the way up to his thighs - he struggled to sleep more than a few hours each night. With money scarce and Western medicine failing, he asked to go to the village where he was born to visit a traditional healer or, if that failed, to be buried next to his parents.Kouassi traveled by bus, which typically takes more than six hours to cover the 200 kilometers, much of it on a choppy dirt road. Years earlier, before heat storms shattered his livelihood, Kouassi had built an eight-bedroom house there with a large patio, where he relished visits from relatives and neighbors, some whispering hush-hush stories. His sons hoped the more comfortable environment and traditional remedies might help him regain his health.The healer took 90,000 CFA, a little less than $160, then refused any more payments even though he kept bringing clay pots filled with medicinal concoctions. But his father continued to decline, Jules recalled, and finally pulled his son aside and asked him "to take care of the family because he didn't know if he would survive." Kouassi died on October 27, 2024, aged 68. No official cause of death was given.His beloved cocoa farm has not recovered. Many of the trees are dead or sick, Jules said, and revenue remains in a rut. Kouassi himself lies buried under a blank headstone, his family unable to afford the finishing tribute: a name plaque. Nor have they been able to raise enough money for a traditional funeral, a fact that torments Jules. In the culture of their Baoule ethnic group, the failure to hold that ceremony - complete with a sheep sacrifice, drumming and dancing - means his father cannot go peacefully into the afterlife. "It's like his soul is still walking around here," Jules said, "unable to rest."FEBRUARY, 2026: A MASSIVE NEW HEAT STORMOver its lifetime, Heat Storm Vera drifted over nearly 85% of the planet, more than any heat storm on record. Its peak size, covering 31.3% of the Earth on January 5, 2024, was also a record. Until this summer.Heat Storm Raimundo, which broiled Europe and stoked massive wildfires in Spain and France, extended over 33.8% of the globe on August 28. Since its inception on February 28, 2026, Raimundo has touched almost three quarters of the planet's surface.Both heat storms spent time over a melting Nepalese glacier before its collapse on August 26 and the catastrophic flooding that followed, killing thousands. Early indications suggest that warming temperatures contributed to the collapse of the glacier and the bedrock beneath it.Up until the glacier gave way, it had spent about 58% of this decade in a heat storm or heat wave, up from 7% during the 1960s. For the six days immediately preceding its collapse, the glacier had been blanketed by Heat Storm Raimundo.Raimundo isn't yet finished. It has been heating the earth for 235 days and counting.
